q: A 23-year-old stabbed in the left chest has absent breath sounds on the left, JVD, tracheal deviation, and hypotension. Most likely:
why: Tamponade also causes JVD and hypotension, but breath sounds stay equal. Absent breath sounds on one side point to tension.

q: Which finding best separates tension pneumothorax from cardiac tamponade?
options: Absent breath sounds on one side
why: JVD, hypotension, and tachycardia happen in both.

q: Tracheal deviation in tension pneumothorax is:
options: A late sign, pushed away from the injured side
An early sign, toward the injured side
An early sign, away from the injured side
why: Don't wait for it to act.

q: A 58-year-old has had chest pressure at rest three times this week, each episode longer than the last. This is:
why: At rest and worsening = unstable. It's part of ACS and treated like a possible MI.

q: A patient with known stable angina has chest pain that doesn't go away with rest and his own nitro. This is:
why: Pain that breaks his usual pattern is ACS until proven otherwise.

q: The key difference between angina and MI is that in MI:
why: Angina is ischemia with no permanent damage; infarction is tissue death.

q: A patient sitting bolt upright has crackles in both lungs and pink frothy sputum after a previous MI. This is:
options: The left ventricle failing, backing fluid into the lungs
The right ventricle failing, backing fluid into the legs
why: Left-sided failure causes pulmonary edema.

q: An 82-year-old was normal yesterday; today she's confused, can't focus, and her alertness comes and goes. This is:
why: Delirium is sudden and fluctuating; dementia develops over months to years.

q: For a patient with sudden delirium, which bedside check rules out a fast, reversible cause?
why: Hypoglycemia is a top cause of sudden ALOC and is quick to fix.

q: A 19-year-old with RLQ pain says it suddenly got better an hour ago. Now his whole abdomen is rigid and he has a fever. This is:
why: Sudden relief followed by diffuse pain and fever is the classic rupture pattern.

q: On a domestic call, the patient is calm but a man behind you is pacing and getting louder. You should:
options: Keep an exit, alert your crew, and be ready to stage and call PD
Focus on the patient; he's not your concern
Ask him to calm down and keep treating
why: Look, think, predict, act — the scene is changing.

q: You ask, 'What were you doing when the pain started?' Which part of SAMPLE is this?
'I take metoprolol and a baby aspirin every morning' fits which part of SAMPLE?
Correct order when a cell doesn't get enough oxygen:
options: Anaerobic metabolism, lactic acid, acidosis, cell death
Aerobic metabolism, CO2 buildup, cell death
Lactic acid, anaerobic metabolism, cell death

q: Byproducts of aerobic metabolism are:
why: Lactic acid comes from anaerobic metabolism.

q: Which action violates HIPAA?
options: Posting a scene photo where the patient can be identified
Giving report to the ED nurse
Telling the receiving doctor about the patient's HIV status
Sharing records under a court order
why: Sharing with treating providers is allowed.

q: A heavy, cyanotic 64-year-old smoker has a wet cough with thick sputum for years and rhonchi. This is:
why: 'Blue bloater.'

q: Which finding points to emphysema rather than chronic bronchitis?
A farmworker has pinpoint pupils, drooling, wheezing with heavy secretions, and HR 44. You should:
why: Patients with organophosphate poisoning drown in secretions (DUMBELS).

q: Which finding does NOT fit organophosphate poisoning?
options: Dilated pupils with hot, dry skin
why: Hot, dry, dilated is the anticholinergic picture — the opposite.

q: A woman 16 weeks pregnant is bleeding and has passed tissue. What do you do with the tissue?
options: Collect it and bring it to the hospital
why: The hospital needs to evaluate it.

q: A 4-month-old is found unresponsive with rigor and dependent lividity. You should:
options: Not start CPR, support the family, and preserve the scene
Start CPR only if parents ask
Move the infant to the ambulance for CPR
why: Lividity and rigor are definitive signs of death.

q: Which is a known SIDS risk factor?
options: Sleeping face down on soft bedding

q: During a code, a new EMT notices the BVM isn't connected to oxygen. Under crew resource management, you should:
options: Say it clearly to the team right away
Fix it quietly without telling anyone
Assume the medic meant to do that
why: Clear communication beats rank.

The Glasgow Coma Scale assesses:
options: Eye opening, verbal response, motor response

Which is a contraindication for nitroglycerin?
why: Nitro drops preload — a low BP will crash.

q: A patient took nitroglycerin with no relief after 3 doses. You should:
why: Unrelieved chest pain = likely MI, time is muscle.

q: The maximum number of nitro doses before transport is:
why: Don't delay transport giving endless nitro.

q: Aspirin dose for suspected cardiac chest pain:
why: Chewed for faster absorption.

q: Which patient should NOT get aspirin?
why: Allergy is an absolute contraindication.

Beck's triad (JVD, muffled heart sounds, hypotension) indicates:
Treatment for cardiac tamponade in the field:
options: Rapid transport — it needs a hospital procedure
why: Pericardiocentesis is a hospital procedure.

q: A narrow pulse pressure suggests:
why: Falling systolic with rising diastolic narrows the gap.

q: Pulsus paradoxus (big BP drop on inhalation) is seen in:
why: Exaggerated normal variation from impaired filling.

q: The most common cause of cardiac arrest in adults:
PEA means:
options: Organized rhythm on the monitor but no pulse

q: Which rhythms are shockable?
Asystole on the monitor — you should:
The purpose of defibrillation:
options: To stun the heart so a normal rhythm can restart
To give energy to the patient

q: After ROSC, you should:
options: Keep the patient still, monitor, and transport
why: Post-arrest patients are fragile — gentle handling.

q: Targeted temperature management after cardiac arrest:
options: Is done in the hospital, not the field
Means packing in ice in the ambulance

A patient with a tracheostomy tube that is blocked:
options: Suction and if that fails, remove and replace the tube
why: A blocked trach is an airway emergency.

q: The main risk of hyperventilating a patient:
options: Blowing off too much CO2, causing vasoconstriction

q: End-tidal CO2 (capnography) during CPR:
options: Confirms tube placement and CPR quality
why: Good compressions = higher EtCO2.

q: A sudden drop in EtCO2 during CPR suggests:
options: The tube is displaced or CPR quality fell

q: A sudden RISE in EtCO2 during CPR suggests:
why: The heart is moving blood again.

q: Normal EtCO2 range:
Waveform capnography is the gold standard for:
why: Continuous waveform = continuous confirmation.
